assessment.nobel_worthiness: The optical lattice clock combines Katori's magic-wavelength idea with Ye's demonstration of unprecedented accuracy and stability. It brought clock uncertainty to the 1e-18 level, enables tests of fundamental constants and relativistic time dilation over millimetres, and opens the way to a redefinition of the second. This is atomic physics where precision reveals new physics, and I can judge the underlying atomic-structure and systematic-shift calculations directly.
assessment.attribution: The two credited names are the natural pair. Katori proposed the magic-wavelength lattice trapping; Ye's JILA group drove strontium and later systems to record performance. Other groups (PTB, NIST, SYRTE) matter, but the two proposed laureates carry the central contributions.
assessment.maturity: Multiple independent laboratories have reproduced and surpassed each other's results, and the interpretation is stable. Recognition is timely; earlier clock-related prizes (frequency combs in 2005, ion control in 2012) laid groundwork without covering this invention.
uncertainties: Whether the committee wishes to wait for the SI redefinition of the second to complete the story.
Overlap with earlier clock-related prizes may weigh on novelty, and the roles of ion-clock groups remain a possible attribution question.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: The 1995 Cirac-Zoller proposal for a trapped-ion quantum gate, together with the later cold-atom and optical-lattice quantum-simulation proposals, supplied the theoretical blueprint that experiments in my field have followed for thirty years. The ideas are original, clear and have had lasting influence across AMO physics and quantum information.
assessment.attribution: Two credited names give a clean configuration for the theoretical contribution, which experimentalists such as Wineland and Blatt then realised. The theory/experiment split is something the committee must justify, but I would not add experimentalists here.
assessment.maturity: Experimental realisation by many independent groups confirms the proposals. The 2012 and 2022 prizes did not cover this theory, so timing seems fair, though crowding with those awards is possible.
uncertainties: Whether the prize is better framed as trapped-ion computing alone (B022 includes Blatt) or together with optical-lattice quantum simulation.
Possible perception that quantum information has been recently recognised.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Matter-wave interferometry with atoms demonstrates the wave nature of massive particles and now underpins inertial sensing, determinations of the gravitational constant and fine-structure constant, and tests of the equivalence principle. It is fundamental, precise and close to the quantum-mechanics questions I care most about.
assessment.attribution: Bordé's theory of Ramsey-Bordé interferometry, Pritchard's early atom-optics and interferometer work, and Kasevich's atom-interferometer sensors form a plausible trio. Chu (1997 prize for cooling) and Ramsey (1989) already partly touch the area, so the allocation is delicate and others could be argued for.
assessment.maturity: Decades of confirmation from many laboratories, with precision tests now at high accuracy. Recognition is timely; large-scale applications are still developing.
uncertainties: Overlap with Chu's work and its prior recognition.
Whether the decisive contributions are correctly split among the three credited names.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Bringing a macroscopic mechanical oscillator to its quantum ground state and controlling it quantum mechanically speaks directly to where the quantum-classical boundary lies, which I regard as one of the deepest questions in the field. The work is conceptually clean and links to precision sensing.
assessment.attribution: Cleland (first quantum ground state of a mechanical resonator, 2010), Teufel (sideband cooling in microwave circuits, 2011) and Aspelmeyer (cavity optomechanics, entanglement and quantum control) are credible, but others (Painter, Harris, Regal, Kippenberg) also made decisive contributions, so the configuration is contestable.
assessment.maturity: Independent confirmations exist and the experiments are reproducible, but the field is still young, and the 2025 prize on macroscopic quantum tunnelling in circuits may argue for waiting before a close neighbour.
uncertainties: Contested allocation across several competing platforms.
Proximity to the 2025 prize may argue for waiting.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: The experimental discovery of the Higgs boson in 2012 confirmed the mechanism of mass generation in the standard model, an outstanding result built on decades of detector development. I defer to colleagues on particle physics, but the importance and clarity are beyond question.
assessment.attribution: The 2013 prize recognised the theory. Experimental credit sits with collaborations of thousands; the credited names represent the leadership. Gianotti, Jenni and Virdee are plausible as founding or leading figures, with Della Negra an equally arguable fourth, so the three-person limit forces an unsatisfying choice.
assessment.maturity: Thoroughly confirmed by two independent experiments and by later Run 2 and Run 3 measurements; recognition after more than a decade is timely, if arguably late.
uncertainties: Tradition against crediting large collaborations leaves the allocation among individuals contentious.
I defer to particle physics colleagues on how to weigh individual leaders.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: The quantum spin Hall effect and topological insulators introduced a new class of electronic states characterised by topology and protected edge or surface states. The theory by Kane and Mele and the experimental demonstration by Molenkamp are original and have had a very large influence.
assessment.attribution: Kane and Mele proposed the quantum spin Hall effect in graphene, and Molenkamp's group observed it in HgTe following the prediction of Bernevig, Hughes and Zhang, who are not among the credited names. This omission is a genuine attribution problem for a fair configuration.
assessment.maturity: Broadly confirmed by many laboratories in several materials, with a stable interpretation. The 2016 prize covered earlier topological work, but this specific discovery is mature.
uncertainties: Omission of Bernevig, Hughes and Zhang, and of Fu and Kane for three-dimensional topological insulators, from the credited names.
I defer to condensed matter colleagues on relative priority.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Squeezed light beats the standard quantum limit in interferometry and is now routinely used in gravitational-wave detectors, a concrete demonstration that quantum-noise engineering matters for real measurement. The idea is elegant and the application is proven at LIGO scale.
assessment.attribution: Caves supplied the theoretical proposal for squeezed-state interferometry, Kimble made early experimental squeezed-light generation, and Schnabel developed applications for gravitational-wave detection. Slusher, Walls, Yuen and others also made foundational contributions, so the three-person configuration omits significant credit.
assessment.maturity: Independently confirmed and deployed in GEO600, LIGO and Virgo. Mature, though part of the story is adjacent to the 2017 gravitational-wave prize.
uncertainties: Foundational contributions by people not among the credited names.
Whether the discovery is better treated as part of the gravitational-wave story already recognised.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: The first horizon-scale image of a black-hole shadow gave direct visual evidence for strong-field gravity near compact objects. It is an important synthesis of very-long-baseline interferometry and data analysis, though in my view more an observational achievement than a discovery of new physics.
assessment.attribution: Falcke proposed the shadow-imaging concept and Doeleman led the build-up of the global array. The collaboration is very large, and algorithm, theory and instrumentation contributors were vital, so credit is diffuse.
assessment.maturity: M87* in 2019 and Sgr A* in 2022 give two independent sources and the interpretation seems stable, though polarimetric and dynamical results are still developing. Timing is plausible but perhaps early.
uncertainties: Large collaboration makes individual attribution uncertain.
I defer to astrophysics colleagues on the weight of imaging versus theory.
